name: Spectrum Analyzer

claims.claim_text: A wideband RF spectrum analyser is one of the last big-ticket instruments a general electronics bench acquires, and its price scales with frequency range rather than with any other specification. New units start at roughly $1,500 to $2,000 and climb steeply from there.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're talking probably $1,500 to $2,000
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Horrisonous Holiday Habromania

claims.claim_text: Choose the analyser's frequency ceiling from the fifth harmonic of the highest signal to be measured, not from the fundamental. A bench working at a few hundred megahertz still needs gigahertz coverage to see the harmonic content that causes emissions problems.
claims.quote_verbatim: make sure you get, like, the fifth harmonic of anything you plan to measure
claims.episode_title: Horrisonous Holiday Habromania

claims.claim_text: A serious RF bench is defined by two instruments rather than one: a network analyser and a spectrum analyser, with a tracking generator if the budget allows. Everything else is secondary.
claims.quote_verbatim: to make a nice RF lab, you have to have a network analyzer and a spectrum analyzer
claims.episode_title: Horrisonous Holiday Habromania

claims.claim_text: Secondhand analysers are the affordable route but they are physically enormous, and freight can cost more than a new instrument for anyone outside the major markets. The purchase price is not the whole cost of ownership.
claims.quote_verbatim: more than a brand new one on eBay
claims.episode_title: NASA, WOTW & Modular Design - The NASA Nostalgia

claims.claim_text: Treat sub-$1,000 direct-from-China one-gigahertz analysers advertised with a tracking generator as suspect. The specification is implausible for the price, and some of these designs still ship with a CRT rather than an LCD, which is itself a signal about the vintage of the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're like $600 and they've got a tracking gen as well
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Horrisonous Holiday Habromania

claims.claim_text: Audio spectrum analysers and wideband RF spectrum analysers are separate instrument classes with separate price structures. Owning one says nothing about having the other, and a lab can accumulate several audio-band instruments and still have no RF capability.
claims.quote_verbatim: a wideband RF spectrum analyzer
claims.episode_title: Horrisonous Holiday Habromania

claims.claim_text: For microwave design specifically, the principal instruments are a power meter and a spectrum analyser, with a frequency counter as a possible third. Oscilloscopes matter far less than at lower frequencies.
claims.quote_verbatim: the principal pieces of test equipment that you need are a power meter and a spectrum analyzer
claims.episode_title: An interview with Tony Long - Millimeter Microwave Magician

claims.claim_text: Very old analysers remain usable for real work: a microwave engineer starting a company on a small budget ran a 12.4 GHz instrument built in 1968 that cost $100, then upgraded to a mid-1980s unit. Age matters far less than coverage and calibration for this class of instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have a spectrum analyzer that I bought for $100, and it goes to 12.4 gigahertz
claims.episode_title: An interview with Tony Long - Millimeter Microwave Magician

claims.claim_text: Analyser cost explodes at the top of the frequency range: a 50 GHz instrument costs as much as a supercar, and the vendors in that space are Agilent, Rohde & Schwarz and Anritsu. This is why microwave startups build their labs from second-hand equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: A 50 gigahertz spectrum analyzer will be as much as a Ferrari
claims.episode_title: An interview with Tony Long - Millimeter Microwave Magician

claims.claim_text: Very fast oscilloscopes get little use in microwave work because the signals are sinusoids and nobody is chasing sharp rise times. The waveform shape carries no information there, so the spectrum analyser displaces the scope as the primary instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's always going to be sinusoids, and we're not trying to get sharp rise times
claims.episode_title: An interview with Tony Long - Millimeter Microwave Magician

claims.claim_text: For RF and FPGA development the three instruments that matter are the signal generator, the spectrum analyser and the logic analyser. Oscilloscopes remain useful for power supplies but are cheap enough not to drive the equipment budget.
claims.quote_verbatim: the big three are the signal generators, spectrum analyzer, and logic analyzer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: A capital-starved startup can substitute a spectrum analyser for a dedicated phase noise meter, taking the data down by hand. The measurement is available; only the convenience is missing.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than a phase noise meter, use a, uh, use a spectrum analyzer and tape data by hand
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Direct probing frequently fails to reveal what is radiating from a board. The technique that works is to wand near-field probes, homemade or purchased, over the board while watching a spectrum analyser, building a map of where energy is coming from.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'd often go in with either homemade or purchased near-field probes called E-field or H-field probes
claims.speaker: Alan Wolke
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Alan Wolke (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: Near-field probes come in two forms, E-field and H-field, physically a stub or a loop, designed to respond to near-field rather than far-field radiation. Making loop antennas by hand to fit into tight spaces on a board is standard practice when a commercial probe will not reach.
claims.quote_verbatim: which are either like a loop or a stub type of antenna
claims.speaker: Alan Wolke
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Alan Wolke (Re-broadcast)

claims.claim_text: Most engineers cannot use a spectrum analyser, because electrical engineering education teaches the oscilloscope and the voltmeter and stops there. The instrument is conceptually a different beast, and the skills gap shows up exactly when EMI work begins.
claims.quote_verbatim: Engineers often don't even know how to use a spectrum analyzer
claims.speaker: Henry Ott
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: The fallback for an engineer without analyser training is the FFT function on a modern oscilloscope, which gives some visibility into frequency content. It is a partial substitute rather than an equivalent.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of the new scopes have FFTs on them
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: The real discriminator between a scope's FFT function and a dedicated analyser is the number of frequency bins. Scope FFTs are mediocre because the bucket count is low, so fine structure in the spectrum simply is not resolved.
claims.quote_verbatim: How many buckets do you get, right? And that's what it really comes down to
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Super Tecmo Bug

claims.claim_text: Modern dedicated analysers achieve update rates that make the display feel live, on the order of 50,000 FFTs per second, achieved with dedicated silicon rather than general-purpose processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was doing, you know, 50,000 FFTs per second
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Super Tecmo Bug

claims.claim_text: A software-defined radio with a display add-on can work as a standalone handheld analyser: a HackRF with a PortaPack tuned anywhere across six gigahertz, running about a thousand FFTs per second over a 20 MHz instantaneous span. The tuning range and the instantaneous span are separate numbers and confusing them overstates the instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: just as a handheld spectrum analyzer across six gigahertz of bandwidth
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: The HackRF was deliberately built without an FPGA, on the reasoning that laptop DSP capability had become strong enough that the board only needed to move samples in and out of high-speed USB at the maximum rate. Pushing signal processing to the host is what kept the cost down.
claims.quote_verbatim: the DSP capability in everybody's laptop is, is so impressive these days
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: A twenty-dollar USB digital TV dongle repurposed as a receiver gives a usable spectrum display, including spectrum over time, which is enough to confirm whether a band is genuinely empty or the local station is at fault. It turns an unfalsifiable suspicion into a measurement.
claims.quote_verbatim: it shows the spectrum over time, too
claims.episode_title: PCB Mills, SDR and Oscilloscopes - Flaunting Furbelow Fanciness

claims.claim_text: Cheap SDR hardware belongs in every signals course. Seeing filtering as narrowing onto the darker part of a spectrum display produces a mental shift that mathematics alone does not, and the hardware is now cheap enough that cost is no longer the obstacle.
claims.quote_verbatim: these should be absolutely required in every signals class
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: The standard pedagogical failure is three weeks of Fourier mathematics followed, at the end, by a frequency chart on an analyser that makes the whole idea obvious in seconds. Showing the measurement first supplies the motivation that carries a student through the theory.
claims.quote_verbatim: three weeks of just horrendous math
claims.episode_title: The Secret Life of Circuits with lcamtuf / Michał Zalewski

claims.claim_text: Having a spectrum analyser physically in front of a student while learning Fourier transforms supplies the reference point that abstract instruction lacks. The general pattern is alternating hands-on and theory rather than front-loading either.
claims.quote_verbatim: having a spectrum analyzer in front of me when I was learning four year transforms
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Eater

claims.claim_text: A spectrum analyser built into an oscilloscope may be capped by the scope's bandwidth licence rather than by its own hardware: buy the 100 MHz scope and the analyser is limited to 100 MHz in software even though the front end can do more. Check what the analyser function is bounded by before treating it as a substitute instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you buy the hundred megahertz model, your spectrum analyzer is only a hundred megahertz
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: A bandwidth-limited built-in analyser is still worth having for switch-mode power supply work, where the interesting content sits well below 100 MHz. It is only worthless for RF, and the switch-mode use case is occasional rather than routine.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can use it for switch mode power supply stuff
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Putting real spectrum analyser hardware into every oscilloscope in a range raises the bill of materials enough to lift the entry-level 100 MHz dual-channel model to around $3,300, which puts it out of competition against instruments that omit the feature. Bundling an expensive subsystem across a whole product line taxes the customers who do not need it.
claims.quote_verbatim: their entry level 100 megahertz dual channel scope is now 3,300 bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: The vendor rationale for building analysers into mainstream scopes was market research showing that around 40 percent of new designs contain wireless. The demand is real even where the pricing consequence is unwelcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: 40% of new designs have wireless in them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: The value of a mixed-domain oscilloscope is the hardware that time-correlates the time domain and the frequency domain, letting a digital event be tied to the RF blip it caused. Strip that hardware out to save cost and what remains is a spectrum analyser sharing a box with a scope, whatever the product is called.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't actually tie the two domains together and do synchronous sampling between them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: Resolution bandwidth and span together set the processing load: a 0 to 2 MHz span with a 300 Hz resolution bandwidth filter is a reasonable request that nonetheless forces the instrument to chew through gigabytes. Expect long updates whenever the ratio of span to resolution bandwidth is large.
claims.quote_verbatim: a zero to two megahertz right span with a 300 hertz resolution bandwidth
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: A well-designed analyser stays interactive while a slow sweep runs, letting the operator stop it, move cursors over data already on screen, or change settings. Locking the user interface during a long acquisition is a design fault, not an unavoidable consequence of the processing load; thirty seconds of waiting is acceptable, a frozen keyboard is not.
claims.quote_verbatim: i could still use the control panel right and stop it anytime i want or go into menus and set other things up while i'm waiting
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: A swept analyser visibly updates point by point as it moves across the band, which is a diagnostic in itself: the display tells the operator where in the sweep the instrument currently is. Instruments that compute the whole screen at once behave differently and cannot be read the same way.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can physically see you know it updates each point you know as it sweeps across
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: What a spectrum analyser is physically doing is sweeping through frequencies one at a time, which is the same mechanism a network analyser uses when it injects a swept stimulus and watches how a circuit responds across the band.
claims.quote_verbatim: It is sweeping through different frequencies
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Richard Ginus

claims.claim_text: A spectrum analyser does exactly one thing: it sweeps over frequency and reports how much power is present at each one. Everything else attributed to the instrument is a consequence of that single measurement.
claims.quote_verbatim: it will just tell you what the, how much power there is at every frequency
claims.speaker: Ted Yapo
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ted Yapo

claims.claim_text: A tracking generator outputs a sine wave locked to wherever the analyser is currently sweeping, so when the receiver is looking at 100 MHz the generator is producing 100 MHz. That synchronisation is what turns a passive receiver into a stimulus-response instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: it generates a signal that's in sync with that sweep
claims.speaker: Ted Yapo
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ted Yapo

claims.claim_text: To measure a filter, connect the tracking generator to one side and the analyser input to the other, then read off how much energy gets through at each frequency across the sweep. The result is a response plot showing whether the stopband is down 10 dB or 50 dB and whether the wanted signal still passes.
claims.quote_verbatim: you connect the tracking generator to one side of the filter and you connect the spectrum analyzer input to the other
claims.speaker: Ted Yapo
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ted Yapo

claims.claim_text: A tracking generator plus a spectrum analyser is a scalar network analyser: it measures amplitude only, not phase. That limitation means no Smith charts and genuine ambiguity when measuring purely reactive components, which is where a vector instrument becomes necessary.
claims.quote_verbatim: the scalar part of a scalar network analyzer means is you're just measuring the amplitude
claims.speaker: Ted Yapo
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ted Yapo

claims.claim_text: A concrete driver for building a notch filter is a nearby broadcast transmitter bleeding into unshielded equipment, strongly enough that a recorder picks up a radio station under the intended audio. Proximity to a high-power site is a design constraint on everything in the building, not just on radio gear.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can hear a radio station coming through
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ted Yapo

claims.claim_text: The bench-instrument price collapse is concrete: a 1.5 GHz analyser with a tracking generator arrived at $1,500, a configuration that had been out of reach for an individual shortly before.
claims.quote_verbatim: Which goes for $1,500 and it comes to the tracking generator
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Davidson - Hoodied HP Hijinks

claims.claim_text: The same capability had cost around $12,000 a year earlier, and before that the only route for an individual was a second-hand boat-anchor instrument from an auction site. The change put a first analyser inside a hobby budget for the first time.
claims.quote_verbatim: a year ago, you'd probably have to spend $12,000 to get that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Davidson - Hoodied HP Hijinks

claims.claim_text: An engineer who worked at HP through the transition describes the same collapse from the vendor side: an analyser that had been well north of $10,000 not long before became available for $1,000 to $1,500 from newer entrants.
claims.quote_verbatim: well north of $10,000 not very long ago
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: A judgment from decades inside a test-equipment maker that once built its own front panels and silkscreens: inspiration for the next design comes from being around manufacturing, so a company that outsources production keeps climbing the value pyramid until nothing is left. The argument is about design capability, not cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of your inspiration for the next designs come from being around the manufacturing
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Analyser frequency ceilings are commonly software options over identical hardware: a unit sold at 2.1 GHz may have a front end capable of 3.2 GHz, unlocked by licence. Check the hardware limit rather than the model number when planning headroom.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's 2.1GB for the base model, but the hardware's capable of 3.2GB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Alexa joins the fray

claims.claim_text: The RF front end of an analyser lives inside a milled aluminium block, an islanded section isolated from the rest of the instrument. That physical partitioning is what the price of the instrument largely buys.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the RF voodoo magic, you know, inside the bigger aluminium block
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Alexa joins the fray

claims.claim_text: A complete general-purpose lab can be equipped for under $10,000, including a couple-of-thousand-dollar scope and a couple-of-thousand-dollar spectrum analyser. RF is the discipline that breaks that budget.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can get a really nice schmick lab for under 10 grand
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: In RF the accessories are not a rounding error: one engineer spent $3,000 on cables to go with a $3,000 second-hand instrument. Budget for the interconnect at the same order as the instrument itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: Jeff spent another $3,000 on frigging cables
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: Cutting a ground plane to route a signal across it costs roughly seven decibels of extra radiated emission, measurable on a spectrum analyser. The fix is to patch the signal through a discrete wire, lay a copper patch over the break and restore a solid plane, and the before-and-after measurement is what teaches the lesson.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just changed the signal radiating from the board by about seven decibels
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: A slot cut in a ground plane behaves as a slot antenna. Naming the mechanism is what makes the emission predictable rather than mysterious, and closing the slot removes the radiator.
claims.quote_verbatim: Got rid of your, your slot antenna there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: Failing EMC compliance costs roughly $2,000 per retest with about three weeks between attempts, so blind iteration is financially ruinous. That economics is what makes pre-compliance measurement on a bench analyser worth the instrument's price.
claims.quote_verbatim: am I just going to have to pay $2,000 every three weeks
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: An experienced test-house technician fixed a failing board by finding long traces that looked noisy on a spectrum analyser, cutting them, and adding two ferrites. The pattern generalises: localise the radiating structure first, then apply the smallest mechanical change that kills it.
claims.quote_verbatim: he took his like spectrum analyzer or whatever and found some long traces that seemed a little noisy, cut them, threw some ferrites on there and it passed
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: A technique for iterating on emissions with hands inside the circuit: use the analyser to find which peaks are failing, then tune an ordinary radio receiver to that frequency and work by ear, poking components and hearing the spurious content attenuate. It frees the operator from watching a screen while probing.
claims.quote_verbatim: he would be listening to the sounds coming over the ham radio
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Interference disputes are settled by measurement rather than assertion: told that a wireless system would interfere with the venue's radio microphones, the operators put both on a spectrum analyser and showed the microphones at 850 MHz against a transmitter at 920 MHz. Carrying the instrument turns a policy argument into a fact.
claims.quote_verbatim: showed that the wireless microphones were at, like, 850 megahertz and that they were transmitting at 920
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: A dynamic signal analyser is an FFT instrument aimed at low frequencies, typically the audio band. It occupies the frequency domain like a spectrum analyser but with a range and resolution tuned to a different problem, so the two are not interchangeable.
claims.quote_verbatim: DSAs typically are for really low frequencies, like audio frequencies
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Keyzermas All The Way

claims.claim_text: A modulation domain analyser plots frequency against time, where an oscilloscope plots voltage against time and a spectrum analyser plots amplitude against frequency. That third axis pairing is what lets you watch a frequency source settle: see it commanded to a new frequency, go out of lock, and drift back in.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a device which plots frequency versus time
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: It's a Keyzermas Miracle!

claims.claim_text: Microwave test used to mean building a rack: a spectrum analyser, a signal generator and a noise figure meter behind a switch matrix. The demand now is one instrument that tests everything at once, because switching between boxes costs process efficiency on the production floor.
claims.quote_verbatim: It used to be you'd build a test system with a switch in a spectrum analyzer
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore
claims.episode_title: Microwave measurement with Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Network analysers since around 2012 have absorbed spectrum analysis, modulated-signal measurement and complicated noise figure measurement, moving well beyond swept sine and CW. The boundary between instrument categories has been dissolving from the vector network analyser side.
claims.quote_verbatim: added the capabilities to do spectrum analysis, to do modulated measurements, to do complicated noise figure measurements
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore
claims.episode_title: Microwave measurement with Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Measuring a 50 watt amplifier without destroying the analyser front end requires a specific block diagram of attenuation and coupling ahead of the input. This is a routine hazard in power measurement and the reason published example setups exist.
claims.quote_verbatim: how can you avoid blowing up your equipment?
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore
claims.episode_title: Microwave measurement with Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Modulation type is readable directly from a waterfall display: a chirp-spread system draws slopes sweeping up and down as frequency changes, while a frequency-shift-keyed link sits static at its centre frequency with a bandwidth set by the modulation parameters. Identifying an unknown signal often starts with this visual distinction.
claims.quote_verbatim: You would just see one waterfall, you know, in one static place
claims.speaker: Felix Rusu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Felix Rusu

claims.claim_text: The first thing to do with a new software-defined radio is route the source block into a frequency sink to get a spectrum plot and waterfall, then tune to a known band such as 433 MHz or 2.4 GHz. Within minutes it reveals that domestic thermostats and car tyre pressure monitors are transmitting continuously, each with a unique identifier.
claims.quote_verbatim: you start seeing your thermostat is transmitting
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Derek Kozel

claims.claim_text: A small two-layer demonstration board connected to a scope or analyser makes an abstract specification concrete: it shows that a nominally 20-bit ADC is delivering 12-bit performance and where the missing eight bits went. Ten centimetres a side and two layers is enough hardware to make that point.
claims.quote_verbatim: you paid for a 20 bit ADC and you're only getting 12 bit performance
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary
claims.episode_title: More Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: Production tuning can be automated by reading the analyser over GPIB while stepper motors adjust the inductors, driving the low end and high end of a tuner into specification without an operator. The instrument becomes a sensor in a closed loop rather than a display for a human.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting data from a spectrum analyzer
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Standard lab benches are too shallow for RF instruments. Custom double-depth benches let a full-depth spectrum analyser sit at the back while leaving a working area in front, which is a cheap fix compared with the equipment it holds.
claims.quote_verbatim: You could put a full depth spectrum analyzer on your bench and still, you know, have a work area
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: For timing-critical work such as DSL development, distribute a single reference clock, in one case a GPS-disciplined 10 MHz, to every instrument in the lab over matched-length coaxial cable. Matching the cable lengths is what keeps the instruments phase aligned as well as time aligned.
claims.quote_verbatim: matched length coax cables going all the way throughout the lab
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: A microcontroller PLL that tops out near 270 MHz, with substantial part-to-part variation between about 250 and 290 MHz, may only expose a quarter of that on an output pin because of the clock tree. Transmitting at 900 MHz from such a part therefore means generating around 69.5 MHz as a square wave and using its harmonic content, which is weak but real.
claims.quote_verbatim: it tops out internally at around 270 megahertz
claims.speaker: CNLohr
claims.episode_title: Long Distance with CNLohr-a

claims.claim_text: Older analysers acquire a chunk of data, run FFTs on it and display the result before acquiring the next chunk, so events between chunks are invisible. Real-time analysers close that gap, which matters for intermittent or bursty signals.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's like real time spectrum analyzers as well
claims.episode_title: A 2013 Recap - Year-end Yarn Yakking

claims.claim_text: A consumer toy with a radio in it can be reverse engineered into a working 900 MHz spectrum analyser, which is both a cheap route to an instrument and a better engineering exercise than most coursework.
claims.quote_verbatim: he turned it into a spectrum analyzer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow - Sprauncy Saccadic Spintherism

claims.claim_text: A spectrum analyser built into a dedicated production tester is scoped to one application, such as testing mobile phones, and is useless outside it despite impressive headline coverage. Instruments sold in quantities of tens or hundreds are designed to one customer's test plan.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's useless because it's only designed for testing mobile phones
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Specialized and/or Open Source Test Gear and Dev Boards - Vacation Videography Vorboten

claims.claim_text: Serious coverage is reachable on the used market: 26 GHz laboratory analysers turn up at auction. Watching corporate liquidations is a viable acquisition strategy for instruments that are unaffordable new.
claims.quote_verbatim: E4407Bs for those playing along at home, like 26 gig
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Aussie Bound!

attribution_notes: Several passages carry speaker labels that do not match the content of the answer (interviewer/interviewee boundaries are fused). Where the label was not corroborated by the content, speaker is null.
ep381 and ep513 are flagged attribution_reliable:false in the bundle; no claim here carries a name from those passages.
